historical_timeline.summary: Older brother Jack died in a sawmill accident.
Began taking amphetamines on the road; addiction lasted about a decade.
Hospitalized with internal bleeding; then treated at the Betty Ford Clinic.
Diagnosed with Shy-Drager syndrome, later called a misdiagnosis.
Treated for pneumonia at Baptist Hospital in Nashville.
Described autonomic neuropathy, diabetes, glaucoma, and loss of about 60 percent of his vision in a televised interview.
Died at Baptist Hospital in Nashville of complications of diabetes with respiratory failure.

claims.statement: J. R. (Johnny) Cash was born on February 26, 1932, in Kingsland, Cleveland County, Arkansas, to Ray and Carrie Cash.

Cash died at Baptist Hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, on September 12, 2003; his manager, Lou Robin, said in a statement issued by the hospital that he died of complications from diabetes, which resulted in respiratory failure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Public statement by his manager; the documented basis for the diabetes in this case. Record the death without graphic detail.

claims.statement: Cash's older brother Jack died in a sawmill accident in 1944.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family event; an injury, not a heritable condition.

claims.statement: In 1957 Cash began taking amphetamines to stay awake on a long road trip, the start of an addiction that lasted about a decade; in a 2002 interview he named amphetamines and barbiturates in the 1960s.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Historical substance use made public by Cash and his biographers. It is not a modern diagnosis in this case.

claims.statement: Cash was hospitalized in 1983 with internal bleeding; after recovering he entered the Betty Ford Clinic for treatment.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Historical treatment for substance use; the cited encyclopedia states he remained abstinent afterward.

claims.statement: In October 1997 Cash was diagnosed with Shy-Drager syndrome, an illness similar to Parkinson's disease; in a 2000 interview he said the diagnosis was a misdiagnosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The diagnosis and its withdrawal were both made public by Cash. The case uses the withdrawn label as a teaching point about autonomic failure in diabetes.

source_links.locator: Cash recounts the Shy-Drager diagnosis and its reversal; the rush transcript's dates differ from other reports

claims.statement: Cash later learned he had autonomic neuropathy; in November 2002 he described it as a deadening of the nerve endings in his lower extremities that had taken the strength from his legs, so that he could walk, but not very well.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Self-reported diagnosis; the anchor for the synthetic diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy.

claims.statement: Cash was repeatedly hospitalized for pneumonia in his last years; he was treated for pneumonia at Baptist Hospital in Nashville in February 2001, and in November 2002 he said he had had pneumonia four times in three years.
In November 2002 Cash said about 60 percent of his vision was gone, which he attributed to the neuropathy and the diabetes, and he said he hoped the glaucoma could also be reversed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own lay account; the type and stage of glaucoma and any retinal findings were not made public.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize that orthostatic lightheadedness, leg numbness, and falls in an older adult with long-standing type 2 diabetes fit diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy rather than a prior label of Shy-Drager syndrome; set an individualized HbA1c goal, choose glucose-lowering drugs that avoid hypoglycemia, treat neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and coordinate glaucoma care so that eye drops do not worsen blood pressure, using the CMID diabetes and glaucoma schedules.

documentation.chief_complaint: Endocrinology consultation and four-week diabetes check: lightheadedness on standing and choice of add-on glucose-lowering therapy

hpi.narrative: Mr. Cash is a 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, autonomic and peripheral neuropathy, and severe primary open-angle glaucoma, seen four weeks after his first visit for an endocrinology consultation on the same day as his diabetes check. Metformin was raised to 1000 mg twice daily, atorvastatin was started, and dorzolamide was added to latanoprost four weeks ago. He takes all of them, and metformin causes no stomach upset. His fasting home glucose readings run 140 to 170 mg/dL, with none below 70. He now stands up in stages, has raised the head of his bed, wears waist-high compression, and drinks about 2 liters a day. He is still lightheaded on standing most mornings and after meals, but he has had no further falls since the first visit. He asks again what he really has, since he was once told it was Shy-Drager syndrome.

assessment_plan.display: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetic autonomic neuropathy
assessment_plan.assessment: A fall of 32 mmHg in systolic pressure on standing with a rise of only 4 beats per minute in heart rate shows a neurogenic cause. With long-standing diabetes and length-dependent sensory loss in both legs, the pattern fits diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and the earlier Shy-Drager label is not carried forward in this record. He is still symptomatic despite non-drug measures, and lying pressure is 150/84 mmHg
plan: Start midodrine 2.5 mg on waking, at midday, and mid-afternoon, with the last dose at least four hours before bed
Continue staged standing, head-of-bed elevation, compression, and fluids
Check lying, seated, and standing pressure at each visit

Seated pressure is above 130/80, but with orthostatic hypotension no blood pressure medicine is used

hpi.narrative: Mr. Cash returns for his three-month review, nine weeks after sitagliptin and midodrine 2.5 mg were started and five weeks after his annual wellness visit. His fasting home readings now run 120 to 150 mg/dL, with none below 70. He is less lightheaded than before midodrine, but he still feels faint for a minute or two after getting up in the morning and after lunch, and he has had no falls. He takes the last midodrine by mid-afternoon and has no scalp tingling or trouble passing urine. He has started physical therapy for gait and balance, and the low-vision home visit is booked. He uses both eye drops every day without stinging. No eye pressure check was done between visits. He is writing and recording at home.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Cash is a 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes complicated by autonomic and peripheral neuropathy, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and severe primary open-angle glaucoma, who returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit four weeks after his endocrinology consultation. Sitagliptin and low-dose midodrine were started then. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit, with a family member reading the questions aloud because of his low vision. He stands up in stages, sleeps with the head of the bed raised, and wears waist-high compression; the lightheadedness on standing is less frequent, and he has had no falls since the consultation. His home glucose readings show no values below 70 mg/dL. He uses both eye drops as prescribed and has added no over-the-counter medicines. He is recording at home and writing most days.

referral.question: Type 2 diabetes above goal in a 71-year-old man with autonomic and peripheral neuropathy and orthostatic hypotension. Please confirm whether diabetic autonomic neuropathy explains his lightheadedness on standing, advise on treating it, and help choose add-on glucose-lowering therapy

referral.pertinent_history: Lightheaded on standing, with two falls in six months; he walks with a cane. Seated blood pressure 146/80 mmHg, falling to 112/68 after three minutes standing, while heart rate rises only from 78 to 82. Numb feet with monofilament and vibration sensation reduced to the ankles. He was once told he had Shy-Drager syndrome and wants to know what he really has. HbA1c 8.6 percent on metformin 500 mg twice daily; eGFR 74, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g, vitamin B12 286 pg/mL, TSH and hemoglobin normal. Severe primary open-angle glaucoma with low vision, followed by the eye clinic; dorzolamide added to latanoprost today. No tobacco or alcohol use. Today metformin was raised to 1000 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg was started, and he began staged standing, head-of-bed elevation, waist-high compression, and 2 liters of fluid a day. No blood pressure medicine is used
questions: Is diabetic autonomic neuropathy a sufficient explanation for his orthostatic hypotension, and should the earlier Shy-Drager label be carried forward?
If the non-drug measures are not enough, which medicine do you recommend, and how should we watch for high pressure lying down?
Which add-on glucose-lowering agent is safest, given his risk of unrecognized low glucose, his falls, and his orthostatic hypotension?

assessment.assessment: Systolic pressure falls 32 mmHg from sitting to standing while heart rate rises only 4 beats per minute, the same pattern as at intake: a neurogenic cause. With long-standing diabetes and length-dependent sensory loss, diabetic autonomic neuropathy explains it, and the earlier Shy-Drager label is not carried forward. assessment.assessment: HbA1c 8.6 percent, above an individualized goal below 7.5 percent that suits his age, neuropathy, falls, and low vision. Autonomic neuropathy can blunt the warning signs of low glucose, so insulin and sulfonylureas are avoided. An SGLT2 inhibitor would add fluid loss to his orthostatic hypotension, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist's nausea, slowed stomach emptying, and weight loss are poorly tolerated with autonomic neuropathy; he has no atherosclerotic disease, heart failure, or kidney disease that would make either essential. Sitagliptin carries little risk of low glucose and does not lower blood pressure, and eGFR 72 allows the full dose
